sources.title: Vemuram Myriad Fuzz: Josh Smith's Hybrid Fuzz Beast
sources.h1: Vemuram Myriad Fuzz: The Brass Box That Started Life As Half Of Something Bigger
sources.excerpt: Vemuram Myriad Fuzz guide: the germanium-silicon hybrid explained, the bias trimmer decoded, verified players, tone settings and 2026 buying advice. admin 22 September 2026 22 min read GG-ARTICLE-TOP Almost every fuzz pedal ever built is an argument about one transistor family. Germanium is warm, woolly, temperature-flaky and cleans up like a dream. Silicon is loud, spitty, aggressive and reliable. You pick a side, you buy the pedal, and you spend the next decade quietly wishing it did the other thing on Tuesdays. GG-ARTICLE-AFTER-INTRO The Vemuram Myriad Fuzz refuses to pick. It puts a silicon transistor and a vintage germanium transistor in the same signal path, gives you a knob called Feel to move between their characters, and hides a trimmer inside the enclosure that biases the germanium side to taste. It is hand-built in Tokyo, wrapped in solid brass, and it costs more than most people’s first amplifier. It is also, unusually for a signature pedal, the leftover half of a much stranger machine — and the guitarist whose name is on it has been photographed using it on his own board for years, which is more than can be said for a lot of endorsements. This is the full story: where the circuit came from, what every control actually does, who genuinely plays one, how to dial it in, and whether the brass justifies the invoice. How to Get the Tone ↓ The short version The Myriad Fuzz is a hybrid germanium/silicon fuzz, hand-built by Vemuram in Tokyo in a solid brass enclosure, developed with American blues guitarist and producer Josh Smith. It has four external knobs — Level, Fuzz, Feel and Tone — plus an internal Germanium Bias trimmer. It runs on a 9-volt battery or a standard centre-negative 9 V supply, is true bypass, and draws a startlingly small amount of current. Its selling point is range. At low Fuzz settings with the Feel knob backed off it behaves like a thick, saturated overdrive with enormous output on tap. Wound up, it goes into Big Muff territory without the mid-scoop, and it retains a low end that vintage Fuzz Face circuits simply do not have. It cleans up off the guitar volume knob the way good germanium fuzzes do, but it does it without the volume drop and tonal collapse that usually comes with that trick. As of September 2026 it is a $435-and-up pedal in the United States, with Equipboard tracking an average across merchants of $462 and a spread up to roughly $558. It sits in the top price tier of the fuzz category, and it knows it. Who Josh Smith is, and why the pedal exists The résumé Josh Smith was born in Middletown, Connecticut on 7 October 1979 and raised in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. He picked up a guitar at seven, was playing blues festivals at ten, and was making albums at fourteen. By eighteen he had three records out. At sixteen he toured the United States with his band the Rhino Cats, who released Born Under a Blue Sign and Woodsheddin’ ; at eighteen he formed the trio Josh Smith and the Frost, whose Too Damn Cold was produced by Jim Gaines — the man behind Stevie Ray Vaughan ‘s In Step . At twenty-two he married and moved to Los Angeles, where he became one of the busiest sidemen and session guitarists in the city, cutting tracks for Taylor Hicks, Ricky Fanté and Raphael Saadiq among many others. He now runs Flat V Studios and has produced records for Eric Gales, Joanne Shaw Taylor, Joanna Connor, Reese Wynans, Larry McCray, Marc Broussard, Artur Menezes, Andy Timmons and Joe Bonamassa . Guitar World placed him sixteenth on its 2019 list of the thirty best blues guitarists in the world today; Rock and Blues Muse put him in its top fifteen contemporary blues rock guitarists for 2020. Why a session producer wanted this particular fuzz Smith’s own account of the pedal’s origin is unusually specific, and it is worth quoting because it explains the design brief better than any dealer copy: “The Myriad fuzz started life as one half of my larger Myriad pedal. When it started to become clear how great the fuzz sounded we knew it would need to be released on its own. This is the fuzz I’ve had in my mind for over 10 years.” Ten years of wanting a fuzz, from a man who spends his working life deciding whether a guitar part fits in a mix, produces a very particular set of priorities. He wanted something that would clean up like vintage germanium, because a session player needs one pedal to cover three parts. He wanted a genuine tone control, because fuzz that only works in one room is useless on a deadline. And he wanted volume — “a large amount of volume on tap,” in his words — because the classic Fuzz Face problem is that it barely reaches unity gain and cannot push an amp. What he did not want, and this is the interesting part, was simplicity for its own sake. His own description ends: “It is incredibly tweak-able but never complicated. There is no bad sounds in this pedal. No matter where you set the knobs you get great tone.” Where the Myriad Fuzz came from The big box came first The pedal most people mean when they say “Myriad Fuzz” is the compact four-knob unit. But the name belongs first to a much larger device — the Myriad, sometimes catalogued as the Myriad “Big Box” Wet/Dry Fuzz — which Josh Smith demonstrated at the Vemuram booth at Winter NAMM on 17 January 2020, and which Equipboard dates to 2020 in a brass finish. The Big Box is not really a fuzz pedal. It is a fuzz pedal wearing a routing system. It carries a dedicated effects loop, two outputs, an expression pedal input and a wet/dry mixer, and its control set runs to WET-LV (Fuzz + Loop), MIX, FUZZ-LV, GAIN, TONE and FEEL, plus toggles for OUT2-GND and for sending the fuzz to output 1 or output 2, push switches for loop phase and output 2 phase, and two footswitches — one for the fuzz, one for the loop. Guitar Part’s French review measured it at 140 x 97 x 50 mm and 750 grams and put its draw at 18.1 mA. Smith’s stated goal for it was two-amp creativity: “I wanted a way to be creative in a two amp situation

sources.excerpt: The Vemuram Myriad Fuzz, a collaboration with Josh Smith, is a versatile fuzz pedal blending silicon and vintage germanium transistors. Offering a wide tonal range from spitty to smooth overdrive fuzz, it features a trimmer for germanium bias control, allowing for dynamic and organic fuzz tones. Its design is inspired by the best vintage fuzzes. What Vemuram say about the Myriad Fuzz A collaboration pedal with Josh Smith. The Myriad Fuzz is a hybrid between a Silicon transistor and a vintage Germanium transistor. The range of the tone is very wide and has enough head room to control the fuzz tone from spitty fuzz to a smooth overdrive fuzz. The trimmer allows you to control the Germanium Bias with the FEEL knob which will affect the tone of the fuzz. Josh Smith's Comment "The Myriad fuzz started life as one half of my larger Myriad pedal. When it started to become clear how great the fuzz sounded we knew it would need to be released on its own. This is the fuzz I've had in my mind for over 10 years. A unique fuzz that employ's both Germanium and Silicon transistors. It is incredibly tweak-able but never complicated. There is no bad sounds in this pedal. No matter where you set the knobs you get great tone. It goes from fire breathing silicon to cool warm germanium easily, it cleans up like the best vintage fuzzes, adn is more dynamic and organic than any fuzz has the right to be. It goes from spitty to smooth effortlessly. It also has a large amount of volume on tap and a tone circuit that allows it to really work live. I've wanted this fuzz all my life and thanks to my friends at Vemuram we all now get to enjoy it!!!" www.vemuram.com Myriad Fuzz compared to ...
